subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In chemistry, what is meant by a 'pure' substance?
options: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance
Any liquid that looks clear and colourless
A substance that is safe to eat or drink
A mixture of elements in fixed proportions
questions.explain: In chemistry a pure substance consists of only one element or one compound, unlike the everyday meaning of 'clean' or 'natural'.

questions.q: How is the Rf value in paper chromatography calculated?
options: Distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
Distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance
Distance moved by substance x distance moved by solvent
Distance moved by solvent - distance moved by substance
questions.explain: Rf equals the distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, giving a value between 0 and 1.

questions.q: How does the melting point of a pure substance compare with that of an impure sample of it?
options: A pure substance melts at a sharp, specific temperature; impurities lower and broaden the melting range
A pure substance melts over a wide range; impurities sharpen it
Both melt at exactly the same sharp temperature
Impurities always raise the melting point to a single value
questions.explain: Purity can be checked because a pure substance melts sharply at a fixed temperature, whereas impurities lower the melting point and spread it over a range.

questions.q: A student needs to obtain solid copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution. Which method should they use?
options: Crystallisation
Filtration
Simple distillation to collect the solid
Chromatography
questions.explain: Evaporating the water so the solution becomes saturated and then cooling it allows soluble copper sulfate to form crystals.

questions.q: Which separation technique is used to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid?
options: Filtration
Crystallisation
Fractional distillation
Chromatography
questions.explain: Filtration traps the insoluble solid as residue in the filter paper while the liquid passes through as filtrate.

questions.q: Why can fractional distillation separate two miscible liquids such as ethanol and water?
options: They have different boiling points
They have different colours
One is soluble and the other is insoluble
They have different Rf values
questions.explain: The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates and passes up the fractionating column first, allowing the miscible liquids to be separated by boiling point.

options: A useful mixture with a precise purpose, made by mixing components in carefully measured quantities
A single pure compound made in a laboratory
Any element found in the periodic table
A substance that has only one boiling point
questions.explain: Formulations such as paints, fuels and medicines are mixtures whose components are present in fixed, measured amounts to give the desired properties.

questions.q: In a chromatogram a spot moves 3 cm and the solvent front moves 12 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?
An ionic bond is best described as which of the following?
options: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
A weak force between separate molecules
questions.explain: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between positive and negative ions formed by the transfer of electrons.

options: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
A transfer of electrons from one atom to another
The attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons
A bond only found between metal atoms
questions.explain: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes metallic bonding?
options: Electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons
Sharing of electron pairs between neighbouring atoms
Transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal ions
Weak intermolecular forces between small molecules
questions.explain: In metals the outer electrons become delocalised, and the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the lattice of positive ions and these free electrons.

questions.q: When sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride, what happens to the electrons?
options: A sodium atom loses one electron to form Na+ and a chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl-
Sodium and chlorine share a pair of electrons equally
Chlorine loses an electron to sodium
Both atoms become delocalised in a sea of electrons
questions.explain: Sodium transfers its single outer electron to chlorine, producing oppositely charged ions that attract to form ionic NaCl.

questions.q: Magnesium forms Mg2+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. What is the formula of magnesium chloride?
options: MgCl2
MgCl
Mg2Cl
MgCl3
questions.explain: Two Cl- ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge on one Mg2+ ion, giving MgCl2.

questions.q: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form?
questions.explain: Each carbon atom in diamond bonds covalently to four others, forming a rigid giant covalent structure that makes it very hard.

options: Each carbon atom bonds to only three others, leaving delocalised electrons free to move
It contains freely moving ions
Its molecules are small and can flow past each other
It has a giant ionic lattice
questions.explain: In graphite each carbon forms three covalent bonds, so the fourth outer electron is delocalised and can carry charge through the structure.

questions.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid?
options: The ions are free to move and carry charge only when molten or dissolved
Electrons are released only when the solid is heated gently
The compound turns into a metal when melted
Covalent bonds break to release protons
questions.explain: In a solid the ions are locked in the lattice, but melting or dissolving frees them to move and carry the electric current.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances usually have low melting and boiling points?
options: The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak and easily overcome
The covalent bonds within the molecules are very weak
They contain freely moving ions
They have giant lattices of strong bonds
questions.explain: Only the weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome to melt or boil simple molecular substances, not the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules.

questions.q: Why are pure metals malleable (able to be bent and shaped)?
options: Layers of metal ions can slide over one another
The delocalised electrons hold the ions rigidly in place
The metal contains weak covalent bonds that snap
Ions are held in a fixed giant ionic lattice
questions.explain: The regular layers of positive ions in a metal can slide across each other, so metals can be bent and shaped without shattering.

questions.q: A solid has a very high melting point, does not conduct electricity when solid, but does conduct when molten. What type of structure does it most likely have?
options: Giant ionic lattice
Simple molecular
Giant covalent (like diamond)
Metallic
questions.explain: A high melting point with conduction only when molten or dissolved is characteristic of an ionic compound, where ions become mobile on melting.
